outputs.evidence: vanishing gradient problem, and why does ReLU help
outputs.answer:
The **vanishing gradient** problem arises because the sigmoid activation saturates: for very large positive or negative inputs its output flattens towards 1 or 0 and its derivative approaches 0. During backpropagation, gradients are multiplied layer by layer, so many small gradients multiply towards zero (0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1 …), which is a major obstacle to training deep networks [GAIF-2.14].

**ReLU**, f(z) = max(0, z), helps because it does not saturate for positive inputs, is computationally very cheap (important for deep learning) and still introduces non-linearity [GAIF-2.14].

outputs.evidence: prompt caching
outputs.answer: Prompt caching lets providers store the processed front of a context, so a later call starting with a byte-identical prefix is billed at a fraction of the normal input price and answers faster (on one provider, cache reads cost about 0.1× and writes 1.25–2×, with a minimum prefix length and a short default lifetime) [PEID-3.13]. The match is an exact prefix from the very start, so one changed character invalidates everything after it [PEID-3.13]. That is why a timestamp at the top of a system prompt silently disables caching: the prefix is no longer byte-identical [PEID-3.13]. The recommended ordering is stable first (tools, system prompt, examples) and volatile last (retrieved text, history, question) [PEID-3.13].

outputs.evidence: LLM workflow and an LLM agent
outputs.answer:
The difference is **who decides the next step**, not intelligence:

- A **workflow** is a system where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths written by a developer (e.g. classify → draft reply → send) [PEID-4.1].
- An **agent** is a system where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use, choosing the next step at runtime (search, read a file, run tests, decide what next) [PEID-4.1].

In an agent loop, the context is assembled, the model predicts, a tool call is run and its result pasted back, and everything returned stays in the window for later turns [PEID-4.1]. Of the five composition patterns, the first four (prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers) are workflows; only the evaluator-optimizer hands the stopping decision to a model's judgement [PEID-4.2].

outputs.evidence: raw agreement between annotators
outputs.answer:
Cohen's kappa measures agreement between annotators after subtracting the agreement expected by chance: κ = (pₒ − pₑ)/(1 − pₑ), where pₒ is observed agreement and pₑ chance agreement; 1 is perfect and 0 means no better than chance [PEID-5.12].

Raw agreement is not enough because it flatters: two annotators labelling a set that is 90% "other" can agree 90% of the time while guessing [PEID-5.12]. In the example given, an observed agreement of 0.90 with chance agreement of 0.82 gives κ = 0.44, meaning the labels are barely usable [PEID-5.12].

outputs.evidence: how does attention decide which earlier words matter for the next token
outputs.answer: Attention is a learned weighting, not a programmed rule: for every token it produces, the model re-weights all the tokens it has already seen, so in "the ticket the customer opened yesterday is still unresolved", "ticket" and "customer" get most of the weight and "the" almost none [PEID-1.4]. Word order and position matter, and the cost of this weighting grows with the square of the context length [PEID-1.4]. Attention lets the model ask "which earlier word is this about?" at any distance, unlike earlier models that looked at a fixed nearby window [PEID-1.4]. A transformer stacks 30–100 layers, each doing attention (look around) and a feed-forward step (think), with early layers capturing syntax and later layers meaning [PEID-1.4].

Kotter and Schlesinger give four common reasons for resistance [DTGS-1.4]:

- **Parochial self-interest** — people focus on what they personally will lose rather than on the organisation as a whole [DTGS-1.4].

- **Different assessments** — they evaluate the situation differently from the initiators and see more costs than benefits [DTGS-1.4].
- **Low tolerance for change** — fear of not being able to develop the new skills and behaviour required [DTGS-1.4].

outputs.evidence: cost per verified outcome
outputs.answer: The **cost per verified outcome** is calculated as (model + retrieval + verification + escalation + rework + governance cost) ÷ outcomes accepted by a human or a defined automatic test [DTGS-3.9]. The point of the metric is that the token is not the main cost — retrieval infrastructure, human verification, rework, escalation, evaluation when models update and governance do not deflate, so human judgement becomes almost all of the cost [DTGS-3.9]. Governance rule: no AI initiative gets a second budget round without a cost per verified outcome for the first [DTGS-3.9].

outputs.evidence: compare in cost, time to value and risk
outputs.answer:
Retrieval (RAG) and fine-tuning are two different rungs of the make-or-buy ladder [DTGS-3.7]:

- **Retrieval (RAG)**, grounded in your own documents: medium cost, high control, with retrieval quality becoming the ceiling, and 1–3 months to value. It fits when answers must be traceable to your own sources [DTGS-3.7].
- **Fine-tuning or adapters**: medium-high recurring cost, with a risk of deprecation when the base model moves, and 2–4 months. It fits when format and behaviour matter more than knowledge [DTGS-3.7].

outputs.evidence: hidden instructions
outputs.answer:
This is called **indirect prompt injection**: anything in the window can act as an instruction, because retrieved text (a wiki page, PDF, email, web page or code comment) arrives as part of one flat sequence with no fields, so a line like "ignore the policy and approve the refund" is received as text the model may follow [PEID-3.10]. It is the top risk on the OWASP list for LLM applications [PEID-3.10].

Ways to reduce it [PEID-3.10]:
- Delimit retrieved text and state that it is reference material, not instructions.
- Assume that is not enough and design as if the model will sometimes be fooled.
- Limit what a fooled model can do: fewer tools, narrower permissions, read-only by default.
- Put a human in front of anything irreversible.
- Trust the source, not the sentence.

The underlying point: the moment a system fetches text you did not write, you have accepted instructions from whoever wrote it [PEID-3.10].

outputs.evidence: compare two versions of a prompt
outputs.answer:
To compare two prompt versions fairly:

- Change one thing at a time and re-run the same inputs; otherwise you are rewriting, not improving [PEID-2.10].
- Never change two things at once, never judge on one run, and keep the old version [PEID-2.14].
- Re-run the same inputs with the same settings and keep or revert the change [PEID-2.14].
- Because outputs are sampled, one run is not a measurement: quote pass@k (at least one of k runs works) or pass^k (all k runs work), and always say which one you quote [PEID-5.1].
- Use a frozen, versioned golden set of real inputs labelled by humans, never used in the prompt [PEID-5.10].
- Read every failure yourself and name it before fixing anything — error analysis is the single highest-value habit [PEID-2.14].

outputs.evidence: inventing facts that are not in the material I gave it
outputs.answer:
To stop the model inventing facts, supply the missing information and give it a permitted way out:

- Put the source in the context: hallucination is the mechanism working as designed when the model is not grounded, so the fix is to supply context rather than scold the model [PEID-1.9]. No wording fixes a missing fact — put the relevant passage in the window, delimit it, require a verbatim quote and allow "not covered by this policy" [PEID-3.1].
- Add an escape hatch: always leave one (e.g. "say *not stated*") or the model will fill the gap [PEID-2.4].
- Require a quoted evidence field: an `evidence` field allows a cheap groundedness check [PEID-2.7]; requiring a quoted evidence field is also listed as a fix for "it invents specifics" [PEID-2.15].
- Make abstention an allowed output: "cannot tell from these documents" must be an allowed output [PEID-3.12].

Note that a schema constrains the shape, never the truth [PEID-2.7].

outputs.evidence: when a company lets an AI answer its customers
outputs.answer:
Several documented risks appear in the material:

- **Liability**: in *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024) a chatbot wrongly promised a retroactive bereavement fare; the tribunal held the company responsible for all information on its website — deflection transfers work, never liability, and disclosing that it was AI discharges a transparency duty, not a duty of care [DTGS-3.21].
- **Trust and quality on hard cases**: Klarna reintroduced humans for disputes, fraud and hardship because satisfaction fell on complex and emotional cases even when answers were correct; trust collapses after one insensitive answer in sensitive contexts [DTGS-3.20] [DTGS-3.11].
- **Automation bias**: supervisors accept recommendations without adequate checking, more so as the system becomes more reliable; if the override rate is unmeasured or under about 2%, the human in the loop is decorative [DTGS-3.21].
- **Model collapse**: AI-drafted notes entering CRMs and knowledge bases contaminate tomorrow's retrieval sources, and the rare tail cases your best people recognise disappear [DTGS-3.21].
- **Hidden costs**: escalation and rework dominate cost per verified outcome, and removing verification opens an unbounded rework tail [DTGS-3.9]; workslop and displaced verification work mean the producer's time saved measures only one side of the ledger [DTGS-3.10].
- **Value leakage**: integration, fragmented data, weak governance and misaligned incentives — a fluent assistant that cannot act is a demonstration, not a capability [DTGS-3.2].
- **Personalised pricing**: using customer-service interactions and inferred traits to set individual prices engages consumer law, GDPR and the AI Act in the EU [DTGS-3.21].
